entries.d12dd495745ff922c933fe0166e180e1580d3c02: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.11.16" sID="gen99071" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.11.16">Luke 11:16</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And others tempting sought from him a sign.</hi> Something similar to this is afterwards related by Matthew, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.4">16:4</reference>,) and by Mark, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.8.11 Bible:Mark.8.12">8:11, 12</reference>.) Hence it is evident, that Christ repeatedly attacked them on this subject, so that there was no end to the wickedness of those men who had once resolved <note n="163"> <div sID="gen99073" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui une fois s’estoyent endurcis</foreign>;” — “who had once become hardened.”<div eID="gen99073" type="x-p"/> </note> to oppose the truth. There can be no doubt that they ask a sign, in order to plead, as a plausible pretense for their unbelief, that Christ’s calling has not been duly attested. They do not express such submissiveness as to be prepared to yield to two or three miracles, and still less to be satisfied with a single miracle; but as I hinted a little before, they apologize for not believing the Gospel on this pretense, that Christ shows no sign of it from heaven. <note n="164"> <div sID="gen99074" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que Christ ne leur monstre aucun signe d’enhaut qui soit pour seelet ceste doctrine</foreign>;” — “that Christ shows them no sign from above that is sufficient to seal this doctrine.”<div eID="gen99074" type="x-p"/> </note> He had already performed miracles before their eyes sufficiently numerous and manifest; but as if these were not enough for the confirmation of doctrine, they wish to have something exhibited from heaven, by which God will, as it were, make a visible appearance. They call him <hi type="italic">Master, </hi>according to custom; for such was the appellation given at that time to all scribes and expounders of the law. But they do not acknowledge him to be a prophet of God, till he produce a testimony from heaven. The meaning therefore is: “Since thou professest to be a teacher and Master, if thou desirest that we should be thy disciples, let God declare from heaven that He is the Author of thy teaching, and let Him confirm thy calling by a miracle.”<div eID="gen99072" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99071" osisID="Luke.11.16" type="section"/>
entries.0c0c8ad0cf92ea1f3c86cb0a53318727a0dc2584: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.11.27" sID="gen99041" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.11.27">Luke 11:27</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Blessed is the womb.</hi> By this eulogium the woman intended to magnify the excellence of Christ; for she had no reference to Mary, <note n="154"> <div sID="gen99043" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il ne faut pas penser qu’elle eust regard a Marie</foreign>;” — “we must not suppose that she had reference to Mary.”<div eID="gen99043" type="x-p"/> </note> whom, perhaps, she had never seen. And yet it tends in a high degree to illustrate the glory of Christ, that she pronounces <hi type="italic">the womb that bore him</hi> to be noble and <hi type="italic">blessed. </hi>Nor was the blessing inappropriate, but in strict accordance with the manner of Scripture; for we know that offspring, and particularly when endued with distinguished virtues, is declared to be a remarkable gift of God, preferable to all others. It cannot even be denied that God conferred the highest honor on Mary, by choosing and appointing her to be the mother of his Son. And yet Christ’s reply is so far from assenting to this female voice, that it contains an indirect reproof.<div eID="gen99042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99044" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Nay, rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God.</hi> We see that Christ treats almost as a matter of indifference that point on which the woman had set a high value. And undoubtedly what she supposed to be Mary’s highest honor was far inferior to the other favors which she had received; for it was of vastly greater importance to be regenerated by the Spirit of God than to conceive Christ, according to the flesh, in her womb; to have Christ living spiritually within her than to suckle him with her breasts. In a word, the highest happiness and glory of the holy Virgin consisted in her being a member of his Son, so that the heavenly Father reckoned her in the number of new creatures.<div eID="gen99044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99045" type="x-p"/>In my opinion, however, it was for another reason, and with a view to another object, that Christ now corrected the saying of the woman. It was because men are commonly chargeable with neglecting even those gifts of God, on which they gaze with astonishment, and bestow the highest praise. This woman, in applauding Christ, had left out what was of the very highest consequence, that in him salvation is exhibited to all; and, therefore, it was a feeble commendation, that made no mention of his grace and power, which is extended to all. Christ justly claims for himself another kind of praise, not that his mother alone is reckoned <hi type="italic">blessed, </hi>but that he brings to us all perfect and eternal happiness. We never form a just estimate of the excellence of Christ, till we consider for what purpose he was given to us by the Father, and perceive the benefits which he has brought to us, so that we who are wretched in ourselves may become happy in him. But why does he say nothing about himself, and mention only the word of God? It is because in this way he opens to us all his treasures; for without the word he has no intercourse with <hi type="italic">us, </hi>nor we with him. Communicating himself to us by <hi type="italic">the word, </hi>he rightly and properly calls us to <hi type="italic">hear and keep it, </hi>that by faith he may become ours.<div eID="gen99045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99046" type="x-p"/>We now see the difference between Christ’s reply and the woman’s commendation; for the <hi type="italic">blessedness, </hi>which she had limited to his own relatives, is a favor which he offers freely to all. He shows that we ought to entertain no ordinary esteem for him, because he has all <hi type="italic">the treasures </hi>of life, <hi type="italic">blessedness, </hi>and glory, <hi type="italic">hidden in him, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.2.3">Colossians 2:3</reference>,) which he dispenses by the word, that they may be communicated to those who embrace <hi type="italic">the word </hi>by faith; for God’s free adoption of us, which we obtain by faith, is the key to the kingdom of heaven. The connection between the two things must also be observed. We must first <hi type="italic">hear, </hi>and then <hi type="italic">keep; </hi>for as <hi type="italic">faith cometh by hearing, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.10.17">Romans 10:17</reference>,) it is in this way that the spiritual life must be commenced. Now as the simple hearing is like a transitory <hi type="italic">looking into a mirror,</hi> <note n="155"> <div sID="gen99047" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Autant que l’ouye simple est comme quand on regarde en un mirroir, et que la memoire s’en escoule incontinent</foreign>;” — “since the simple hearing is as when we look into a mirror, and the remembrance of it immediately passes away.”<div eID="gen99047" type="x-p"/> </note> as James says, (1:23,) he likewise adds, <hi type="italic">the keeping of the word, </hi>which means the effectual reception of it, when it strikes its roots deep into our hearts, and yields its fruit. The forgetful hearer, whose ears alone are struck by the outward doctrine, gains no advantage. On the other hand, they who boast that they are satisfied with the secret inspiration, and on this ground disregard the outward preaching, shut themselves out from the heavenly life. What the Son of God <hi type="italic">hath joined let not men, </hi>with wicked rashness, <hi type="italic">put asunder, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.6">Matthew 19:6</reference>.) The Papists discover amazing stupidity by singing, in honor of Mary, those very words by which their superstition is expressly condemned, and who, in giving thanks, detach the woman’s saying, and leave out the correction. <note n="156"> <div sID="gen99048" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et en leurs graces apres le repas, ils prenent le dire de la femme, laissans la correction qui estoit le principal</foreign>;” — “and in their thanksgivings after a meal, they employ the woman’s saying leaving out the correction, which was the most important matter,”<div eID="gen99048" type="x-p"/> </note> But it was proper that such a universal stupefaction should come upon those who intentionally profane, at their pleasure, the sacred word of God.<div eID="gen99046" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99041" osisID="Luke.11.27" type="section"/>
entries.8163c6c79c6479917b5c2e4783294a47459860bf: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.11.30" sID="gen99080" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.11.30">Luke 11:30</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">As Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites.</hi> He declares that he will be <hi type="italic">a sign </hi>to them, as <hi type="italic">Jonah </hi>was to the inhabitants of Nineveh. But the word <hi type="italic">sign </hi>is not taken in its ordinary sense, as pointing out something, but as denoting what is widely removed from the ordinary course of nature. In this sense Jonah’s mission was miraculous, when he was brought out of the belly of the fish, as if from the grave, to call <hi type="italic">the Ninevites </hi>to repentance. <hi type="italic">Three days and three nights</hi> This is in accordance with a well-known figure of speech. <note n="166"> <div sID="gen99082" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quant aux <hi type="italic">trois nuits, </hi>il y a ici (cornme on scait bien) une figure que les Grecs et Latins appellent Synecdoche</foreign>;” — “as to the <hi type="italic">three nights, </hi>there is here (as is well known) a figure which the Greek and Latin writers call Synecdoche.”<div eID="gen99082" type="x-p"/> </note> As the <hi type="italic">night </hi>is an appendage to the <hi type="italic">day, </hi>or rather, as the day consists of two parts, light and darkness, he expresses a day by a day and a night, and where there was half a day, he puts down a whole day.<div eID="gen99081" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99080" osisID="Luke.11.30" type="section"/>
entries.8bfcc3ea333c8d046bcd5f689d51ba26ac4f4394: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.11.37" sID="gen99500" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99501" type="x-p"/>This narrative agrees in some respects, but not entirely, with the doctrine laid down by Matthew, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.1-Matt.10.20">10:1-20</reference>,) that Christ, in order to correct the superstition of the people, and particularly of the scribes, intentionally disregarded outward ceremonies of human invention, which the Jews were too solicitous to observe. God had prescribed in his Law certain kinds of <hi type="italic">washings, </hi>that by means of them he might train his people usefully to the consideration of true purity. The Jews, not satisfied with this moderate portion had added many other washings, and more especially, that no person should partake of food till he had been washed with the water of purification, as Mark relates more minutely, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.12.3 Bible:Mark.12.4">12:3,4</reference>,) and as is also evident from John, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.2.6">2:6</reference>.) This fault was accompanied by wicked confidence; for they cared little about the spiritual worship of God, and thought that they had perfectly discharged their duty, when the figure was substituted in the place of God. Christ is fully aware that his neglect of this ceremony will give offense, but he declines to observe it, in order to show that God sets very little value on outward cleanness, but demands the spiritual righteousness of the heart.<div eID="gen99501" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99500" osisID="Luke.11.37" type="section"/>
entries.71a193336a17e84b9c9c614bd524f886a8d8d5c3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.11.39" sID="gen99502" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">39. </hi><hi type="italic">Now you Pharisees</hi> Christ does not here charge the <hi type="italic">Pharisees, </hi>as in Matthew, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20">15:1-20</reference>,) and Mark, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.12.2-Mark.12.13">12:2-13</reference>,) with serving God in an improper manner by human inventions, and breaking the law of God for the sake of their traditions; but merely glances at their hypocrisy, in having no desire of purity except before the eyes of men, as if they had not to deal with God. Now this reproof applies to all hypocrites, even to those who believe that righteousness consists in ceremonies appointed by God. Christ includes more than if he had said, that it is in <hi type="italic">vain to serve God by the commandments of men, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.7">Mark 7:7</reference>;) for he condemns generally the error of worshipping God by ceremonies, and not spiritually, by faith and a pure affection of the heart.<div eID="gen99503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99504" type="x-p"/>On this point the prophets had always contended earnestly with the Jews; but, as the minds of men are strongly inclined to hypocrisy, they proudly and obstinately adhered to the conviction, that God is pleased with external worship, even when it is not accompanied by faith. But in the time of Christ, they had sunk to such depth of folly, that they made religion to consist entirely in absolute trifles. Accordingly, he directs his accusation against the <hi type="italic">Pharisees, </hi>for being extremely careful to <hi type="italic">wash cups, </hi>and cherishing <hi type="italic">within their hearts the most abominable filth of cruelty and wickedness</hi> He charges them with folly on this ground, that God, who created <hi type="italic">that which is within the man,</hi> his soul, as truly as the body, cannot be satisfied with a mere external appearance. The chief reason why men are deceived is, that they do not consider that they have to deal with God, or, they transform Him according to the vanity of their senses, as if there were no difference between Him and a mortal man.<div eID="gen99504" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.11.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99502" osisID="Luke.11.39" type="section"/>

41. But out of what you have, give alms. Christ, according to his custom, withdraws the Pharisees from ceremonies to charity, declaring that it is not water, but liberality,
“Mais que c’est une prompte affection de faire bien a ceux qui sont en necessite;” — “but that it is an active disposition to do good to those who are in want.”
that cleanses both men and food. By these words he does not disparage the grace of God, or reject the ceremonies of the Law as vain and useless; but addresses his discourse to those who feel confident that God will be amused by mere signs. “It is the lawful use alone,” he says, “that sanctifies food. But food is rightly and properly used by those who supply from their abundance the necessities of the poor. It would therefore be better to give alms out of what you have, than to be careful about washing hands and cups, and to neglect the poor.”
The inference which the Papists draw from these words, that alms are satisfactions, by which we are cleansed from our sins, is too absurd to require a lengthened refutation. Christ does not here inform us by what price we must purchase the forgiveness of sins, but says that those persons eat their bread with cleanness, who bestow a part of it on the poor. I understand the words, τὰ ἐνόντα, to mean “the present supply,”
“Les presentes choses, comme aussi ie l’ay traduit au texte;” — “the present things, as also I have translated it in the text.”
and not, as Erasmus and the old translator render them, “what remains over.”
It seems quite as natural to suppose, with other interpreters, that τὰ ἐνόντα answers to τὸ ἔσωθεν in the 39th and 40th verses Πλὴν (κατὰ) τὰ ἐνόντα will thus be equivalent to πλὴν (κατὰ) τὸ ἔσωθεν (τοῦ ποτηρίου) δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, but as to what is within the cup give alms out of it. The next, clause commences with καὶ, followed by an ellipsis of (κατὰ), τὸ ἔξωθεν (τοῦ ποτηρίου) μὴ μεριμνήσητε, and give yourselves no concern about what is outside of the cup; for, lo, all things are clean to you. —Ed.
The reproofs which immediately follow may be reserved, with greater propriety, for another occasion. I do not think it probable that Christ, while sitting at table, indulged in this continuous strain of invective against scribes and Pharisees, but that Luke has introduced here what was spoken at another time; for the Evangelists, as we have frequently mentioned, paid little attention to the order of dates.

Luke 11:53. And while he was saying these things to them. I have formerly mentioned that the preceding sentences were not inserted by Luke in their proper place. For while he was relating that Christ at a dinner reproved the scribes, he introduced also the latest discourses by which, a little before his death, he reproved their wicked courses; and in like manner, the reproof which we have just now examined is inserted by Luke, in connection with a different narrative. If any one prefer to follow the opinion of those who conjecture that Christ repeated the same discourses on various occasions, I have no great objection. After pronouncing the curses which have been now explained, he concludes by saying that all the scribes became more inveterate against Christ, so that they did not cease to entrap him by ensnaring questions; which ought to be referred to the conversation held at the table, rather than to his latest discourse. But I have not thought it a matter of great importance to be very exact about the time — a matter which the Evangelist has disregarded.

               <ns0:p n="1">1 AND it came to pass, that as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased one of his disciples, said unto him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.<ns0:note place="bottom">This seemeth to be a different time from that mentioned by <ns0:hi>Matthew,</ns0:hi> where our Saviour directed his Disciples to pray, there his direction was part of his <ns0:hi>Sermon on the Mount.</ns0:hi> Besides the doxology or conclusion is there left out. It is said here, as he <ns0:hi>was Praying in a certain place.</ns0:hi> Christ looked upon all places as holy enough for Prayer. It also looks as if at this time our Saviour was not at his more secret Devotions, but with the twelve, (which were his Family) praying with them <ns0:hi>when he ceased.</ns0:hi> This is very observable against those who pretend impulses of the Spirit, to disturb Ministers in the time when they are Praying and Preaching; it may easily be known from what Spirit, such impulses are. The Disciples of Christ often propounded questions to him after Preaching, but never interupting him in his Work, nor before he was retired into an house. As our Saviour's design in the former Words appeareth to be our information, that the the hand of God be full of good things proportioned to all the necessities of his Creatures; yet they must not expect to have them without <ns0:hi>asking,</ns0:hi> he will for them be <ns0:hi>enquired of by the house of Israel, Ezech.</ns0:hi> 36.37. and all his promises for the collation of <ns0:hi>good things,</ns0:hi> must be Interpreted, with a supposition of Peoples <ns0:hi>seeking</ns0:hi> them at his hand, as also that every <ns0:hi>lazy,</ns0:hi> cold formal Praying will not obtain them at the hand of God, but the <ns0:hi>working, fervent Prayer of the righteous availeth much.</ns0:hi> His design in these Verses seemeth to be, to let us <ns0:hi>know, that fervent and importu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nate Prayer,</ns0:hi> will not prevail with God to give us any thing, but what shall be <ns0:hi>good for us</ns0:hi>; for he knoweth that the general desire of our Souls, is for nothing but what is good, if we ask for things hurtful, it is but a <ns0:hi>lapse</ns0:hi> or miscarriage of our Tongues, caused from the blindness and ignorance of our Minds. Our Saviours speech in these verses, is plainly both <ns0:hi>Elliptical</ns0:hi> (something being in it self to be understood) and also <ns0:hi>Metaphorical.</ns0:hi> The sense is this, what the Eye is to the Body, that the <ns0:hi>Soul,</ns0:hi> the Mind and Affections are to the whole Man. Now look as the <ns0:hi>Eye</ns0:hi> is the <ns0:hi>Organ,</ns0:hi> by which light is received to guide a Mans steps, so that if that be perfect without any mixture of ill humors, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> the Body from it takes a full and right direction how to move and act. But if that be vitiated by ill humours, the Man knows not how to direct his bodily steps.                </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 And the Lord said unto him, Now do ye Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Tit. 1.15.</ns0:note> but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 Ye fools, did not he that made that which is without, make that which is within also?<ns0:note place="bottom">We have much the same tho delivered in another form, with a denuntiation of a <ns0:hi>Woe, Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.25. See the Notes on that <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> We must not imagine that our Saviour here reflecteth upon the cleansing of Vessels, in which we put our Meat and Drink, for un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doubtedly as to them, the Pharisees washed both the inside, and the outside. And the conceit of them is amiss who think that by the inward part, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 39. <ns0:hi>he means the Meat in their Dishes,</ns0:hi> which was gotten indeed, by <ns0:hi>ravening,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Wickedness, Extortion,</ns0:hi> &c. for it is an hard Interpretation of the <ns0:hi>inward part of the platter,</ns0:hi> to say, by it is meant, <ns0:hi>the Meat in the platter</ns0:hi>; but neither doth our Saviour say, <ns0:hi>the inward part of the Dish,</ns0:hi> but your <ns0:hi>inward part,</ns0:hi> by which he plainly means the Soul. Our Saviour doth therefore certainly compare the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Dishes</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Platters,</ns0:hi> washed, or scoured only in the outside; and blameth their <ns0:hi>Hypo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crisie</ns0:hi> in this; That they were mighty sollicitous about an outside purity, and cleanness; but for the inward purity of the <ns0:hi>Heart and Soul,</ns0:hi> they took no care at all about that; they were very scrupu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lous about undefiled hands, but nothing at all about having their Souls, and inward Powers, and affections undefiled. This he telleth them was most egregious folly, for God that made the Body, made the Soul also, and therefore would exact a purity in the inward, as well as the outward Man, especially considering that he <ns0:hi>loveth truth in the inward parts.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 <ns0:note place="margin">1 Isa. 58.7. Dan. 4.27. Chap<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 12.33.</ns0:note> But rather give alms of such things as you have: and behold, all things are clean unto you.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.<ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>as you are able.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>] The Word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> being a Word not ordinarily used in a sense which will fit this place, hath made a great abounding in their own senses amongst Interpreters. Some translating it, <ns0:hi>Give such things as are within for Alms,</ns0:hi> others, <ns0:hi>such things as you have,</ns0:hi> others, <ns0:hi>such things as are ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessary,</ns0:hi> others, <ns0:hi>such things as ye are able,</ns0:hi> as if <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> were to be understood before <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> according to what you have. O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>What things remain,</ns0:hi> after the <ns0:hi>serving your own neces<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sities,</ns0:hi> and a <ns0:hi>just</ns0:hi> restitution to those whom you have wronged. Others think it is but a Connexion of our Saviours Speech, and the Sense is, <ns0:hi>Moreover there is but one thing to be done, Give Alms,</ns0:hi> &c. as if it were <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. I do not see but our own Tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slation is as good as any, and <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> seems to be understood in the <ns0:hi>Greek<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> According to what you have,</ns0:hi> which is truly, and justly your own, not theirs whom you have wronged, nor your Creditors, nor your Families for their necessities, <ns0:hi>Give Alms of all that</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> And behold <ns0:hi>all things are clean unto you.</ns0:hi> Not <ns0:hi>your Souls are clean,</ns0:hi> tho that must first be yet our Saviour is not here directing that, or the Means and Methods for it, but <ns0:hi>all things are clean to you</ns0:hi>; you may lawfully and without Guilt use them, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.15. <ns0:hi>Vnto the pure, all things are pure, but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure.</ns0:hi> Our Saviours Words are a plain Exhortation to <ns0:hi>Repentance,</ns0:hi> that lyeth in the <ns0:hi>change of our minds,</ns0:hi> and that inward change of our minds, must be evidenced by the Change of our Actions, and particularly by a <ns0:hi>Restitution</ns0:hi> in Case of wrong done to any. The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> were a Covetous Rapacious Generation, full of <ns0:hi>Extortion, devouring Widows Houses,</ns0:hi> &c. Their Repentance was to be evidenced by <ns0:hi>contrary Works</ns0:hi>; those were Works of <ns0:hi>Iustice</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mercy.</ns0:hi> God calleth to the <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>aelites</ns0:hi> for the first, <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 1.16, 17. Christ calls to the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> for the latter. Such Works of Mercy as might evidence their Hearts to be truly chan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged, and then saith our Saviour, all <ns0:hi>things will be clean to you,</ns0:hi> which otherwise will not be with all your <ns0:hi>Traditional Supersti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s Washings.</ns0:hi> And needs it must be so, for no Soul can <ns0:hi>Repent</ns0:hi> truly without the Influence and A<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>istance of Divine Grace, which God giveth not, but to those Souls which are Washed with the Blood of Christ. So that before a Soul can produce the Fruits of true Repentance, it must be justifyed by Faith, and Sancti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fyed by the Spirit of Holiness. Or if we understand it only of that <ns0:hi>Repentance,</ns0:hi> which an <ns0:hi>unjustifyed, Soul</ns0:hi> may have, yet even that may so far profit, as to have our outward things so blessed to us, that we may use them without any Pollution or Guilt, and have them outwardly blest to us.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:309" />42 But wo unto you Pharisees, for ye tithe mint and rue and all manner of herbs, and pass over judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment and the love of God, these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.23. There are two great Notes of Hypocrites. 1. To be more exact in, and Zealous for the obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation of <ns0:hi>Rituals</ns0:hi> and the Traditions of men, than in and for the observation of the <ns0:hi>Moral Law of God.</ns0:hi> 2. In matters of Morali<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty to be more exact, and strict in, and for little things, than for things more grave and weighty. There is no Commandement of God so little as we may neglect, or despise, or disobey it, but yet there is a difference in Duties, and we ought to have a first re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gard to the greater, than to the lesser.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 Wo unto you Pharisees, for ye love the up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />permost seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 23.6, 7. Their fault was not in their taking them, but in their affecting them, and in being Ambitious of them. God is the God of order, and we are bound to give <ns0:hi>honour, to whom Honour</ns0:hi> belongs, but <ns0:hi>Pride</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ambition</ns0:hi> are detestable Sins, especi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally in such as should be <ns0:hi>Teachers</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Humility,</ns0:hi> and the Vanity of all things below.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 Wo unto you scribes and pharisees, hypo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crites, for ye are as graves which appear not, and the men that walk over <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> are not aware <ns0:hi>of them.</ns0:hi>
                  <ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.27. where our Saviour compa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reth the Pharisees to <ns0:hi>whited Sepulchres,</ns0:hi> here he compareth them to <ns0:hi>Sepulchres,</ns0:hi> but not as there to denote their Hypocrisy, ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearing <ns0:hi>white,</ns0:hi> but having nothing within but <ns0:hi>Rottenness</ns0:hi>; but upon the account of the Contagion of them, and their <ns0:hi>Polluti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on</ns0:hi> of others that were not aware of them. To understand our Saviour, we must consider the Levitical Law, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 19.16. where we shall find that not only he that tounched a dead Body, but he that touched a Grave was <ns0:hi>Legally unclean for seven Days.</ns0:hi> Christ here alludeth to that, tho he be speaking not of <ns0:hi>Legal,</ns0:hi> but Moral uncleanness. By reason of the Law afore-mentioned, the Jews took care to <ns0:hi>white their Graves,</ns0:hi> that People might see them, and avoid that danger. To such whited Sepulchres, Christ compares the <ns0:hi>Pharisees, Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.27. But <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ome <ns0:hi>Graves</ns0:hi> might not be whited, or the Colour washed off, so as they did not appear, and Men could not be aware of them, but ran into a Pollution by them. To such Graves he in this place compares them. They were Men that Externally appeared not to be what they were. The Jews took the Pharisees for great Saints (the strictest Sect of their Religion) so strict they were in their Du<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties to their <ns0:hi>Traditions, &c.</ns0:hi> which External Severity and for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mal behaviour, covered their Extortion, and Covetousness, and Malice, and Erroneous opinions, so as People did not suspect them of any such Guilt.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">45 Then answered one of the lawyers, and said unto him, Master, thus saying, thou reproachest us also.<ns0:note place="bottom">This Lawyer was a <ns0:hi>Scribe of the Law, v.</ns0:hi> 44. The Work of these Men was to interpret the Law, the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> strictly obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved their Decrees, and Interpretations. The Lawyer therefore spake rightly in thinking our Saviours Words, had some reflecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on upon Men of his order, but he wofully erred both in think<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his own order was unblamable, and also in calling our Lords just Reproof a Reproaching them. But by this he gives an oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion to him, who used rightly to divide the Word of God, and to give every one their Portion out of it, to let them know wherein they were faulty, as well as the Pharisee<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 And he said, Wo unto you also ye lawyers, for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be born, and ye your selves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.4.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 Wo unto you, for ye build the sepulchres of the prophets, and your fathers killed them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">49 Therefore also said the Wisdom of God, I will send them prophets and apostles, and <ns0:hi>some</ns0:hi> of them they shall slay and persecute:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="50">50 That the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired of this generation;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 4.8.</ns0:note> From the blood of Abel unto the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Chro. 24.20, 21.</ns0:note> blood of Za<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />charias, which perished between the altar and the temple: verily I say unto you, it shall be required of this generation.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.29. to <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 37. The <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> like a company of wretched Hypocrites, under a pretence of their honouring the Memories of the Prophets, under the Old Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stament, took a great care to Repair, and to Adorn their Sepulchres, while in the mean time, their Hearts were as full of Malice against the Truth, and against Christ, and those who came to reveal Gods Will to them, as ever were their Fathers against the Prophets, and saith our Saviour, I, who am the Wisdom of God tell you, that I shall send you Apostles, and Prophets, and some of them you shall Kill, others you shall Persecute; that all the Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous Blood that hath been shed on the Earth, from the Blood of <ns0:hi>Abel,</ns0:hi> to the <ns0:hi>Blood</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Zacharias,</ns0:hi> may come on you, which mind being in you, the same as in your persecuting predecessours, your Building, and Adorning the Old Prophets Tombs, is not (as you would have it thought) any Testimony, of your <ns0:hi>Honour</ns0:hi> to the Prophets; But rather to <ns0:hi>your Fathers</ns0:hi> that killed them, a kind of <ns0:hi>Trophey</ns0:hi> for the Victory your Fathers got over the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets of the Lord; so as by that Act you give a <ns0:hi>Testimony,</ns0:hi> that you own them, as your Fathers who killed the Prophets, and glory in what they did, for if you truly honoured their Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mory, you would not retain the same Malicious bloody Mind. It is gross Hypocrisy for Men to magnify the Servants of God in former Ages; and in the mean time to Malign and Persecute the Servants of the same God, in a present Age, owning but the same Truths, and living up to the same Rule. See further Notes on what is in these Verses, in the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.29. where the same things are said with larger Circumstances. They truly Honour <ns0:hi>Martyrs,</ns0:hi> that live the same Lives they did, and adhere to the same Truths of God, in a Testimony to which they Dyed.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="52">52 Wo unto you lawyers, for ye have taken a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way the key of knowledge: ye entred not in your selves, and them that were entring in, ye hindred <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>forbad.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 23.13. <ns0:hi>For you shut up the Kingdom of Heaven against Men,</ns0:hi> &c. I take the Sense of these Words to be, you have taken away Knowledge, which is the <ns0:hi>Key</ns0:hi> by which Men enter into the Kingdom of God. Tho Know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge it self be but a common Gift, and Men may have great Measures of it, and yet perishfor ever, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.2. yet it is the Foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dation of all saving Grace, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.14. <ns0:hi>How shall they be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve on him, of whom they have not heard?</ns0:hi> So how shall they obey a rule they do not know, or <ns0:hi>Repent</ns0:hi> of those Sins, which they do not know to be so. So as those that are the hinderers of Peoples coming to the Knowledge of the Will of God, are the vilest Instruments upon Earth in hindring Men, and Womens Salvation. The <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> are highly guilty of this, in keeping their Laity from the Scriptures in a Language intelligi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to them. But how were the Scribes guilty of this? The Jews were never hindred from <ns0:hi>Reading,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>hearing of the Law.</ns0:hi> It was read in their Synagogues every Sabbath Day. But we must know that <ns0:hi>Knowledge</ns0:hi> is highly advantaged by an Inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pretation of the Mind and Will of God: But how did the Scribes take away this? They Preached and Interpreted the Law of God. <ns0:hi>An.</ns0:hi> They gave not the true Sense of it, but so Preached, that People were scarce any whit the wiser, as to the Knowledge of the Law of God, only they made People understand their Traditions, and Ceremonies: their Doctrines were the <ns0:hi>Traditions of Men.</ns0:hi> Now they occupying the places of Teachers, and no better discharging their Work, instead of giving, took away know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge from them, and proved blind<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Leaders of the Blind. Who<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever they are that arrogate to themselves the Office of Teaching, and supplying the place of Teachers, and either do not make Preaching, and instruction of the People under their charge, their business, or who Preach in Stiles, and Methods their People under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand not; or who Preach other things, than what they prove to be the revealed Will of God, fall deeply under the Condemnation of this Text.—See further the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.13.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="53">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:310" />53 And as he said these things unto them, the scribes and the Pharisees began to urge <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> vehement<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, and to provoke him to speak of many things.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="54">54 Laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him.<ns0:note place="bottom">Herein the Vile Genius of these wretched Men was seen, Christ was become their Enemy, because he told them the Truth. His Reproofs in order to their Reformation, and amendment do but fill them with madness against him. Nor are Wicked and Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />litious Men at any time fair Enemies, <ns0:hi>they urge him Vehemently.</ns0:hi> and provoke him to speak many things, they lye at the Catch, in wait for him; hoping that in his many Words, and Answers to their many Captions questions, they should hear something from him, upon which they might form an Accusation against him, to <ns0:hi>Pilate</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Roman Governour,</ns0:hi> for his Blood was that they Thirsted after. If it were thus done to the Green-Tree, let us not wonder if it be so done also to the dry. The Hearts and Practices of Malitious and Wicked Men, in succeeding Generati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons do (as in a Glass) answer the Hearts of Persons of their Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rits, and Morals in preceding Generations. Malice will never re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gard Justice or Equity.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
